content: 1. Store the sample at room temperature. 2. In neonates and infants, nasopharyngeal aspirate (NPA) has a 15% higher isolation rate compared to nasopharyngeal swab (NPS). 3. Before collecting the NPA sample, select a location in the household that is least used by the family. 4. Place a clean paper towel on a surface to hold the equipment. 5. If the subject is a child and is being held by a parent, ensure the parent is wearing a mask. 6. Once the subject is properly positioned for the NPA procedure, wear gloves. 7. Remove the equipment from its bag and place it on the clean paper towel. 8. Loosen the cap of the sterile container but do not open it until the catheter tip is ready to be inserted. 9. Open the syringe and remove the plastic tip. 10. Attach the syringe securely to the end of the catheter and test the syringe. 11. Remove the catheter from its wrapper. 12. Gently and slowly insert the catheter into one nostril, rotating it if necessary, to pass beyond the back of the nostril. 13. Insert the catheter until it reaches the back of the throat, approximately 10 cm deep, depending on the subject's age. If gagging occurs, the catheter has been inserted too far. 14. After positioning, withdraw the catheter with suction by placing your thumb over the suction control on the catheter while pulling back on the syringe plunger. 15. After removing the catheter from the nose, without touching its tip, open the sterile container and place the catheter tip inside. 16. Screw the top of the container on while the catheter and syringe are still attached to protect the tubing containing the specimen. 17. Label the sterile container, place it along with the catheter and syringe in a plastic bag, and seal the bag. 18. Remove the gloves and dispose of them in a plastic bag. 19. Transport the NPA specimen appropriately. Serum Sample Collection 20. Obtain a serum collection kit before collecting the sample. 21. Follow standard precautions during the procedure. 22. Properly label the blood collection tube with the subject's name, unique identifier (UID), and date of collection. 23. Using an acceptable venepuncture technique, collect 2–3 mL of whole blood. 24. Allow the blood to clot for at least 15 minutes. 25. Centrifuge the sample to separate the serum from the clot. Alternatively, store the whole blood sample overnight in an upright position in a refrigerator at 2–6°C. 26. Properly label a 2-mL plastic storage tube for the serum collection. 27. Store and transport serum samples at 2–8°C. Pertussis Diagnostic Notes 28. Culture of nasopharyngeal secretions is the most specific diagnostic test for pertussis. 29. Since Bordetella pertussis is highly sensitive to drying, specimens should be inoculated onto culture media without delay. 30. Regan-Lowe agar or freshly prepared Bordet-Gengou medium is typically used for culture. 31. The fastidious growth requirements of B. pertussis make it challenging to isolate. 32. The likelihood of isolating the organism decreases if: Specimen collection is delayed beyond the first two weeks of illness (catarrhal stage). The patient has received appropriate antibiotic therapy. The patient has been vaccinated. 33. The optimal time for culture-proven diagnosis is during the catarrhal phase when the etiology of the infection is not yet suspected, leaving a narrow window for diagnosis. Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) 34. PCR is a valuable tool for the timely diagnosis of pertussis. 35. It detects DNA sequences of the bacterium and does not require viable bacteria in the specimen. 36. However, PCR may yield false-positive results. 37. The test has optimal sensitivity during the first three weeks of coughing, as bacterial DNA is present in the nasopharynx during this period. 38. After four weeks of coughing, the amount of bacterial DNA diminishes rapidly. Serological Testing 39. Serological testing can be useful for diagnosing pertussis after four weeks of cough onset. 40. Enzyme immunoassays to detect IgA and IgG antibodies to pertussis toxin, filamentous hemagglutinin, pertactin, and fimbriae are increasingly important diagnostic tools. Surveillance and Reporting 41. Surveillance systems should ensure completeness and timeliness of reporting, with a target of over 80% of designated sites reporting data, even in the absence of cases. 42. Adequate investigation includes completing a case investigation form, collecting nasopharyngeal or serum specimens, and listing close contacts. 43. Specimen transport to laboratories should occur within two days of collection, with results reported promptly. Vaccination and Epidemiological Data 44. Vaccination history, including type and dates of doses, should be documented. 45. Epidemiological data, such as contact with confirmed cases or recent travel history, should be collected for case classification and outbreak investigation. Acknowledgments 46.
